title: Tokyo Court Protects Human Voices in AI Clone Case
paragraphs: A Tokyo court has awarded legal protection to the human voice after a popular anime voice actor demanded that TikTok close an account over its unauthorized use of an AI clone of his.
The Tokyo District Court's decision on September 30 was the first acknowledgment of the right to one's voice in Japan.
The ruling was good news for anime voice actors at a time when they are increasingly concerned about the use of AI-generated versions of their voices on social media.
The case ruled in favor of Kenjiro Tsuda, who plays Kento Nanami in the popular Jujutsu Kaisen series, and is known for his deep voice.
Tsuda said that the anonymous owner of a TikTok account called "Nanami" wrongfully profited by using his voice in more than 180 videos, and asked for the material to be deleted.
As of November 2025, the account had more than 200,000 followers, with viewers often noting the similarities between the narrator's voice and Tsuda's.
In a court document, Judge Aya Takahashi said the account's use of Tsuda's cloned voice with the intention to take advantage of its commercial appeal was "an infringement of publicity rights."
The defendant argued that the videos didn't use Tsuda's voice, just an AI-generated voice that sounded like his, and that the videos didn't damage Tsuda's professional reputation.
While the court ruled in favor of Tsuda, his demand that all the videos using his voice be deleted was dismissed because the account had already been closed.

The use of AI-generated voices that sound like public figures has become a topic of debate in recent years. In 2024, OpenAI ended the use of one of its ChatGPT voices after actor Scarlett Johansson said it sounded similar to hers.

However, some actors see AI as a business opportunity. Last year, Oscar-winning actors Michael Caine and Matthew McConaughey made deals with ElevenLabs to allow its AI technology to clone their voices.
